title: 272. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Graphing Cube Root Functions
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Domain of a Cube Root Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain of a basic cube root function.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\)?
questions.explanation: The cube root of any real number is defined because every real number has a real cube root. For example, \(\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27}=3\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Recall that unlike square roots, cube roots are defined for negative numbers as well as positive numbers.

questions.concept: Domain of a Shifted Cube Root Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain of a cube root function after a horizontal shift.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-2}\)?
questions.explanation: The cube root is defined for every real number, so no restriction is imposed by the radicand \(x-2\). For any real number \(x\), \(x-2\) is a real number and its cube root exists. Therefore the domain is all real numbers, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: A cube root does not require its radicand to be nonnegative.

questions.concept: Range of a Shifted Cube Root Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of a cube root function after a vertical shift.
questions.question: What is the range of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}+3\)?
questions.explanation: As \(x\) varies over all real numbers, \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) also takes every real value. Adding \(3\) shifts the output, but the set of possible outputs is still every real number. Therefore the range is all real numbers, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: The cube root function has no maximum or minimum output value.

questions.concept: Key Point of a Shifted Cube Root Graph
questions.learningObjective: Identify the key point of a cube root graph from its equation.
questions.question: What is the key point of the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x+1}\)?
questions.explanation: The key point of the parent cube root graph \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) is \((0,0)\). For \(y=\sqrt[3]{x+1}\), the radicand is zero when \(x+1=0\), so \(x=-1\). At that value, \(y=\sqrt[3]{0}=0\). Therefore the key point is \((-1,0)\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Set the radicand equal to zero to find the \(x\)-coordinate of the key point.

questions.concept: Horizontal Shift of a Cube Root Graph
questions.learningObjective: Describe the horizontal shift of a cube root function.
questions.question: How is the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) shifted to obtain the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-4}\)?
questions.explanation: The equation \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-4}\) is in the form \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-h}\) with \(h=4\). A positive \(h\) shifts the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) to the right by \(4\) units. Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: In \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-h}\), the graph shifts \(h\) units horizontally.

questions.concept: Comparing Domains of Cube Root and Square Root Functions
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the domain of a cube root function from that of a square root function.
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the domains of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) and \(y=\sqrt{x}\)?

options.label: B
options.text: The cube root function has domain all real numbers, while the square root function has domain \(x\ge 0\).

questions.explanation: The cube root function is defined for every real number, including negative numbers. The square root function is defined only when the radicand is nonnegative, so its domain is \(x\ge 0\). Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: Consider whether the function is defined for negative input values.

questions.concept: Vertical Shift of a Cube Root Graph
questions.learningObjective: Describe the vertical shift of a cube root function.
questions.question: How is the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) shifted to obtain the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}+5\)?
questions.explanation: The equation \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}+5\) has the form \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}+k\) with \(k=5\). A positive \(k\) shifts the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) upward by \(5\) units. Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: The number added outside the cube root indicates a vertical shift.

questions.concept: Writing a Shifted Cube Root Equation
questions.learningObjective: Write the equation of a cube root function from its key point.
questions.question: A cube root graph has key point \((2,1)\). Which equation could represent the graph?
questions.explanation: A cube root graph with key point \((h,k)\) has equation \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-h}+k\). For \((2,1)\), we need \(h=2\) and \(k=1\), so the equation is \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-2}+1\). Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: Substitute the key point into \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-h}+k\) and solve for \(h\) and \(k\).

questions.concept: Range of a Reflected Cube Root Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of a reflected and shifted cube root function.
questions.question: What is the range of \(y=-\sqrt[3]{x}+2\)?
questions.explanation: As \(x\) varies over all real numbers, \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) takes every real value. Negating and then adding \(2\) still produces every real value because the cube root already spans all real numbers in both directions. For example, to obtain very large positive outputs, choose very negative \(x\). Therefore the range is all real numbers, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Consider what values \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) takes as \(x\) ranges over all real numbers, then apply the reflection and shift.

questions.concept: Describing Transformations of a Cube Root Graph
questions.learningObjective: Describe the horizontal and vertical shifts of a cube root function.
questions.question: How is the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x}\) shifted to obtain the graph of \(y=\sqrt[3]{x+3}-2\)?
questions.explanation: The expression \(x+3\) can be written as \(x-(-3)\), so the horizontal shift is left \(3\) units. The \(-2\) outside the cube root indicates a vertical shift down \(2\) units. Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: Rewrite \(x+3\) as \(x-(-3)\) to determine the direction of the horizontal shift.
